name: content-based-router
intent: Route each message to the one destination whose consumer can handle it, by evaluating the message's own content against explicit routing rules, so the decision lives in a single maintained routing component instead of being re-derived by every receiver.
problem: One logical input stream carries work belonging to several different back-ends - orders per region, events per type, requests per priority - and destination and content are merely correlated, not addressable from each other. The producer would have to know the whole topology and pre-sort its output, every new destination makes that pre-sorting more wrong, and each receiver ends up re-inspecting the payload to decide whether the message is even for it.
context: Message-based integration - in-process pipelines, broker topologies, API edges - where several destinations exist for one logical message type and the choice depends on data the message itself carries (a discriminator field, a region code, an amount threshold, a priority header), while the rules themselves are fixed at build or configuration time. If the rules must change per message or at runtime without a redeployment, the pattern to reach for is the Dynamic Router, not this one.
benefits: Producers stay decoupled from the topology: they send to one logical input channel and never learn how many destinations exist or who owns them.
New destinations, and new rules for existing ones, are added in one component - the router - without touching producers or unrelated receivers.
The routing decision becomes an explicit, inspectable artifact (a rule table, a DSL route, a broker rule) instead of being scattered across consumers' type checks and if/else chains.
Receivers can be specialised: each destination's handler deals with exactly the message shapes it is meant for, on the narrowest possible contract.
Rules can be ordered, reviewed and tested as data, so the routing matrix (destination x rule) becomes a testable surface rather than emergent behaviour.
The topology can change independently of the message contract: adding a region, splitting a queue or moving a destination to another service changes rules, not messages.
Centralised routing logic simplifies auditing and compliance: all routing decisions flow through one observable component that can be monitored, logged and traced end-to-end.
In service mesh contexts (Istio, Envoy), content-based routing via VirtualService rules lets platform teams enforce routing policies without application code changes.
tradeoffs: The routing function is the pattern's named maintenance hotspot: every new destination and every rule change lands in one component that all traffic crosses, so it attracts change faster than anything around it (the EIP catalog calls this out explicitly).

Routing rules encode assumptions about the payload schema; when a producer renames or retypes the discriminator, the router silently misroutes or falls through to the default instead of failing loudly - coupling that few stacks check at compile time.

Without a fallback destination an unmatched message is silently dropped, so the pattern forces an explicit unroutable-message decision (Invalid Message Channel, Dead Letter Channel) that is easy to forget and hard to notice.

Broker rule languages usually see message properties or headers rather than the body (verified for Azure Service Bus: filters cannot evaluate the message body), so 'route on the payload' quietly degrades into 'route on whatever the producer promoted to a property'.

The router inspects and usually deserializes every message to make its decision: it becomes a shared latency and CPU hop on the hot path of the whole flow, and parse-twice (route, then process) is a real cost.
Rule sets drift into an undocumented business-rules engine: the fallback branch accumulates meanings ('everything else') and nobody can say why a given message went where it went.
Testability is only as good as the rule representation: hard-coded conditions leave the destination x rule matrix untested, and the failing cases are exactly the ones nobody thought of.
Routing and delivery are separate steps: a router that decides and then fails before the send duplicates or loses messages unless the send is idempotent or the routing step transactional.
With many destinations the rule matrix can become a form of hidden business logic that is difficult to govern - similar to an ever-growing if/else funnel that nobody wants to touch.
Schema evolution without versioning: adding a new discriminator value can silently fall through to an unexpected destination instead of triggering an explicit migration path.

A CBR can become a centralised bottleneck in high-throughput paths - every message must pass through it, and complex predicates or external lookups inside routing logic directly impact tail latency across all destinations.

participants.responsibility: Sends each message to one logical input channel and stays unaware of how many destinations exist or which rules apply; its only obligation is that the routing-relevant fields are present and promoted to accessible locations (header or body).
participants.notes: Should explicitly promote discriminator fields to the routing surface (header for broker-based routing, accessible field for in-process routing). In service mesh contexts, this means setting appropriate headers (e.g., x-tenant-id, x-api-version) before the router evaluates them.

participants.responsibility: Decodes the message, evaluates the routing rules in order, selects the destination channel and forwards the message unchanged; it owns the decision, not the work.
participants.notes: Must remain stateless and free of side effects. Never mutate, enrich or transform the payload inside the router. In Apache Camel, use choice() with when/otherwise predicates; in Spring Integration, use a Router component with explicit mappings. In Istio/Envoy, a VirtualService with HTTP match rules implements this at the mesh layer.

participants.responsibility: The ordered conditions (predicate rows, DSL branches, broker rules) that map message content to a destination; the versioned artifact to review and test whenever destinations change.
participants.notes: Expressed as data rather than embedded code. Each rule should be named, ordered, and have a single destination. Rules should be reviewed as a matrix: discriminator value → destination. In WSO2 Integrator, use a Match node for pattern-based routing (stable keys) and If nodes for predicate-based routing (dynamic thresholds). In Istio, HTTP match blocks are evaluated top-to-bottom (first match wins).

participants.responsibility: The output channel, queue, topic, service endpoint or mesh subset for one destination; the router's only knowledge of the receiver is this binding.
participants.notes: Channel names should be centrally defined constants, not inline strings inside rule predicates. In service mesh deployments, destinations map to Kubernetes service subsets (e.g., v1, v2) defined via DestinationRule.

participants.responsibility: The destination for messages no rule matches - an Invalid Message Channel, Dead Letter Channel or explicitly named default - so a routing gap is observable instead of silent.
participants.notes: Monitor this channel's volume; a rising rate is the earliest signal of schema drift or rule misalignment. In Apache Camel, the otherwise clause covers unmatched messages; in Spring Integration, configure a default-output-channel.

use_cases: Regional or tenant routing: one order stream split per region or tenant because each back-end owns its own data and must not see the others'.
Classification in a canonical pipeline: invoices to finance, cancellations to a reversal service, high-value orders to manual review, everything else to standard fulfilment.
Partner or protocol edge: each partner dialect or payload version is dispatched to a version-specific handler, so a legacy handler keeps receiving exactly its shape.
Priority routing: messages whose content indicates an SLA breach or a premium customer bypass the bulk queue and go to the expedited channel.
Broker-level dispatch: AMQP headers exchanges, JMS message selectors and Service Bus subscription rules implement the pattern inside the broker so the application never sees the irrelevant traffic.
Event fan-in in an in-process pipeline: one stream of heterogeneous commands is dispatched to the branch that handles each kind, keeping every branch's contract narrow.
Unroutable-message handling: content no rule recognises is sent to an inspection channel instead of being retried forever against a destination that cannot process it.

Multi-cloud or multi-region routing: based on message attributes (e.g., data residency requirements, x-region header), messages are routed to region-specific processing endpoints or cloud-specific backends.

Regulatory routing: messages containing specific data categories (PII, financial, health) are routed to compliance-mandated processing or audit destinations; for example, PCI-DSS scoped messages to a secure lane, HIPAA-scoped messages to a PHI-compliant processor.

API Gateway tenant routing: SaaS or multi-tenant APIs route incoming requests to tenant-specific backends based on API keys, tenant IDs in JWTs, or header values (e.g., x-tenant-id → tenant-specific upstream).

Event mesh distribution: in a distributed event mesh, events of different schemas or domain origins are routed to appropriate consumer groups based on event type or source system; for example, domain events routed to domain-specificSaga State Machines.
Log and telemetry fan-out: observability pipelines route logs or traces to different destinations (SIEM, data lake, real-time analytics) based on severity, service name, or environment.

GraphQL operation routing: requests are routed to different backend services based on the GraphQL operation type or name in the request body (e.g., mutations to a write service, queries to a read service) - useful when the gateway cannot determine the target from the URL alone.

gRPC method routing: in microservices using gRPC, the router inspects the :path or :method headers to route to the appropriate backend service when a single gRPC gateway fronts multiple backend packages.

Istio/Envoy service mesh traffic shaping: VirtualService HTTP match rules route requests to specific service subsets (v1 vs v2) based on custom headers, enabling canary deployments and progressive traffic shifts without application-level routing logic.

AWS API Gateway routing: regional REST APIs route requests to different Lambda functions or ECS services based on the request body, headers, or HTTP method, enabling a single API endpoint to serve multiple backend implementations.

Kafka Streams substream split by event field — one input topic split into per-genre output topics using split().branch(pred, Branched.withConsumer(ks -> ks.to(...))), with a literal true catch-all branch as the explicit default (Confluent vendor tutorial).

Dynamic branches generated from a closed enum in Kafka Streams — one branch per RecordType value built in a loop, so the routing table is derived from the enum rather than hand-written string comparisons.

Enrich-then-route pattern with Kafka Streams — orders joined with a GlobalKTable of customer data, then routed to platinum/gold/silver/bronze topics by loyalty level, so the decision uses external data without putting a lookup inside the router.

Ballerina healthcare appointment routing — a single REST resource receives a reservation payload and routes on hospital_id to three hospital back-ends, keeping each backend unaware of the front door (official WSO2 integration tutorial).

Ballerina partner/county tracking routing — a tracking request routed by a typed union (UK/DE) to two different carrier APIs with different response shapes, the wildcard case returning an error rather than silently mapping to a default destination (official Ballerina EIP page).

NServiceBus command routing by assembly/namespace/type — RouteToEndpoint at the type level selects the destination endpoint from the message's declared identity, with per-type routes overriding namespace routes overriding assembly routes.

NServiceBus periodically refreshed route table as data — a FeatureStartupTask timer calls UnicastRoutingTable.AddOrReplaceRoutes so centralized or DB-driven route information updates without redeploying the endpoint.

MassTransit per-message destination resolution — AddMessageRoute<T>((provider, message) => new Uri(...)) computes the queue from the message instance at send time, enabling a slow-lane queue under load.

MassTransit routing slip for per-transaction itineraries — a routing slip built per transaction with payment method, billing address and customer preferences as the routing data, combined with saga state machines for monitoring and compensation.

Camel route-template + precondition deploy-time branch — one parameterized route family where the branch is selected from property placeholders at route initialization, contrasted with content-based when() predicates evaluated per message.

AWS SNS payload-based routing with FilterPolicyScope: MessageBody — a single REST endpoint dispatches to Lambda functions or SQS queues based on nested JSON payload fields, with separate metrics for unmatched versus malformed payloads.
Azure Event Grid advanced data-field filters on detail.* fields — routing Blob storage events by container name or numeric operators (NumberIn, NumberLessThan) without parsing the full event body.

Amazon EventBridge event-bus pattern matching on event metadata and detail body fields — one event bus receives events from multiple sources, with rules dispatching to different targets based on source, detail-type and detail.state, with the Sandbox for pre-deployment testing.

Azure Service Bus autoforwarding chain for subscription scale-out — a first-level topic with subscriptions forwarding to second-level topics to stay within the 2,000-subscription cap while maintaining per-region routing graphs (4-hop chain limit applies).

Google Cloud Pub/Sub multiple subscription filters on one topic — each subscription carries a different filter expression so different consumer groups receive only relevant events, with non-matching messages auto-acknowledged.

AWS IoT SQL rules over MQTT message streams — messages evaluated via SQL SELECT/WHERE and republished to S3, DynamoDB, SQS, Lambda or Step Functions based on payload content, with Basic Ingest bypassing the broker for cost-sensitive paths.

FHIR R4 subscription-based routing with id-only payloads — routing notifications to clinical systems using only resource IDs rather than full resources, limiting disclosure surface (recommended in FHIR security considerations).

PHI routing to HIPAA-eligible AWS services — SNS, SQS, EventBridge, MSK and Lambda marked as HIPAA-eligible are the only valid destinations for ePHI-bearing messages; the router's destination set encodes compliance eligibility.

Smart order router under best-execution duty — FIX protocol ExDestination field carries the routing decision as an auditable artifact, with the router required to document venue selection rationale per FINRA Rule 5310 and SEC Rule 606 disclosures.

PCI DSS scope reduction via routing into a segmented cardholder data environment — the CBR is the enforcement point that keeps PAN-bearing flows inside the CDE boundary and must avoid writing PANs into rule conditions, logs or routing attributes.

LLM request routing as an economic CBR — RouteLLM-style routers decide per request between a strong and a weak model to cut cost (>2x reported) without degrading quality; routing decisions become statistical and failure modes are quality regressions.

Semantic router for vLLM — a model classifies queries by reasoning requirements and selectively applies reasoning only when beneficial; the discriminator is a learned embedding rather than a header or discriminator field.

Istio fragmented VirtualService with a single catch-all — when a VirtualService is split across resources, only one catch-all rule should exist as all catch-alls are moved to the end of the merged list and whichever is applied first disables the others.

Envoy scoped routing by tenant-derived scope key — a scope key computed from a request header selects an independent route table per tenant, enabling tenant-shaped routing without one growing rule list.

Apache ActiveMQ message selectors — JMS subscriptions filter with SQL-92 expressions over headers and properties (JMSType = 'car' AND color = 'blue' AND weight > 2500), implementing broker-side content-based routing so consumers never see irrelevant traffic; XPath selectors additionally evaluate XML message bodies (official ActiveMQ selectors documentation).

Mule EIP mapping — MuleSoft's official EIP documentation maps Content-Based Router to the Mule Choice router, which evaluates expressions against the message payload and attributes to dispatch each event down exactly one route.
avoid_when: The decision does not depend on message content - the destination is already known from the channel the message arrived on, or every consumer needs every message: use plain addressing or a Publish-Subscribe Channel.
The rules must change per message or at runtime without a rebuild: that is the Dynamic Router (rules supplied from outside), not this pattern.
The message must go to every named receiver rather than one: that is a Recipient List (the receiver set is data).
The job is to remove fields or reshape the payload rather than to choose a destination: that is a Content Filter or Message Translator, applied at the destination.
There is exactly one destination and one handler: a router with a single rule is an indirection without a decision; call the handler directly.

The decision genuinely needs the body but the only available rule language can see properties: promote the discriminator at the producer, or keep the router in-process instead of pretending the broker inspected the payload.
The routing logic is genuinely business process logic (complex branching, calculations, time-based conditions): that belongs in a process orchestrator or a rules engine, not a content-based router.

The message volume is extremely high and the router would be on every message's hot path with complex predicates: consider pushing routing to the edge (producer-side header tagging) or using broker-native filtering to avoid a centralised CPU bottleneck.
anti_patterns: 'If/else funnel': one router accumulating every business rule of the enterprise, so changing any business process means editing the component all traffic crosses.

'Router as transformer': mutating, enriching or reformatting the payload on the way through, so destination-specific needs leak into the shared routing component (that work belongs to a Content Enricher or Message Translator at the destination).
'No fallback': rules without an otherwise/default branch, so unmatched messages are dropped silently and the routing gap stays invisible until someone asks where the traffic went.
'Route on a private field': rules that depend on an internal identifier no published contract promises, so a producer refactor re-routes traffic with no interface change.
'Re-check per consumer': every receiver re-inspects the payload to decide whether it should handle the message - exactly the state the router exists to remove.
'Broker rule over the body': writing a rule-language condition against a payload field the broker cannot see (Service Bus filters cannot read the body) and assuming messages will match.

'Rule as code': embedding routing logic in if/else chains or switch statements rather than in a declarative rule table, making the routing matrix invisible to business reviewers and untestable without deploying the router.

'Silent schema drift': when a producer evolves its schema and the discriminator value changes format or disappears, messages silently fall through to the fallback destination, corrupting its contract without any alarm.

'Synchronous lookup inside routing': calling an external service (e.g., a rules database or directory) synchronously from inside the routing predicate, creating a latency spike on every message and a new failure mode (the lookup service being down).

'Hub-and-spoke bottleneck': using CBR to create a star topology where all traffic flows through one central router, turning it into both a maintenance hotspot and a single point of failure under high load.
design_principles: Single responsibility: the router selects a destination and forwards; it does not process, transform or enrich.
Open/closed: a new destination is a new rule or binding, not an edit to every consumer or to the producer.
Separation of concerns: the routing decision (where) is separated from the processing decision (what), which each destination owns.
Explicit contracts over implicit conventions: routing rules are a versioned, reviewed artifact, not tribal knowledge spread across consumers.
Fail fast and fail visibly: an unmatched message reaches an observable fallback instead of disappearing.
Immutable routing rules during processing: rules are versioned at build or deploy time; runtime adaptation belongs to the Dynamic Router.
Failover-first design: always define a fallback route; an unroutable message in production is a data quality incident, not a routing bug.

Promote discriminators to the routing surface: producer-side header/property promotion ensures that both in-process routing and broker-level filtering can see the discriminator without needing to parse the full body.

Parse once, route with structured data: decode just enough to extract the routing fields into a structured form; pass that structured form to the rule evaluator rather than reparsing the raw message for every predicate.
best_practices: Always define a fallback destination and monitor its volume; a rising fallback rate is the earliest signal that rules and payload schemas have drifted apart.
Express rules as data (table, configuration, route DSL) so the destination x rule matrix can be unit-tested and reviewed like code.
Validate and extract the discriminator once, before routing; the router should receive a decoded value, not raw bytes.
Keep the router stateless and side-effect free: no per-message mutation, no enrichment, no logging of full payloads.
Give every rule a named destination and keep the names in one place; a channel name that exists only as a string inside a condition will eventually be wrong.
Order rules deliberately and document first-match-wins; broad conditions belong last, immediately before the fallback.
Test the matrix, not the happy path: one case per destination plus one unmatched payload, and a regression test for every misrouting incident.
Prefer compile-checked dispatch (sealed types, discriminated unions, tags) over string comparison of discriminators whenever the message set is closed.
If the broker routes, confirm which part of the message the rule language can see (usually headers/properties, not the body) and promote the discriminator explicitly at publish time.
Version the rule set alongside the message schema; a rule that worked for schema v1 may silently break for v2.
Instrument the router: emit structured logs or traces with the rule evaluated, the match result and the chosen destination - this is the only way to debug why a message went somewhere unexpected.
When the rule set grows beyond a handful of conditions, extract routing into a separate configuration artifact (JSON, YAML, database table) and treat it as a governable business artifact, not code.

For closed message sets, use type-based dispatch (PayloadTypeRouter in Spring Integration, sealed class matching in Kotlin/Scala, discriminated unions in TypeScript) so the compiler catches unhandled cases.

In Apache Camel: use precondition mode only when predicates are independent of message content; for content-based routing prefer standard when() predicates evaluated per message. Combine with Route Templates for parameterized, optimised routing.

In Spring Integration: always configure default-output-channel for unroutable messages; set resolution-required=false if channel lookup failures should be gracefully handled rather than throwing an exception.
In service mesh deployments (Istio/Envoy): prefer exact header matches over regex for high-throughput paths; always include a catch-all route block at the bottom of the VirtualService/match list.

Prefer GraphQL or gRPC method-level routing at the API gateway rather than body-parsing in the router when the operation type/name is available in the request metadata (headers for gRPC, operation name for GraphQL).

When routing rules must encode business thresholds (e.g., amount > 50000), externalise the threshold values to a configuration artifact rather than embedding numeric literals in rule predicates; this allows rules to be updated without a code deployment.

For high-throughput scenarios, evaluate whether the router can be bypassed for the majority of traffic by tagging the destination at the producer (producer-side routing), reserving the router only for exceptional cases.

Consider routing rule ordering carefully with WSO2-style Match nodes: evaluate pattern-based routing (stable discriminator values) first, then predicate-based routing for threshold or range conditions.

Model content routing as split(Named.as(prefix)) + branch(pred, Branched.withConsumer(ks -> ks.to(topic))) and always terminate with an explicit default branch; use Named.as()/Branched.as() so branch names appear as named processors in the topology and are visible in Topology.describe() and metrics.
Never emulate a Recipient List with split(): branching is first-match and assigns each record to one branch only; to send one record to several outputs apply one filter() per destination.

Keep branch predicates pure and allocation-light: branching is a stateless record-by-record operation on the hot path; any external lookup belongs in an upstream enrichment step (table lookup, GlobalKTable) rather than inside the predicate.

Generate branches from a closed set where possible (one branch per enum value, as the Kafka Streams javadoc dynamic branching example demonstrates) instead of hand-writing string comparisons; the enum documents the routing matrix.

Before upgrading to Kafka Streams 4.x, migrate KStream.branch() (deprecated since 2.8, removed in 4.0) to split(); 4.0 removes APIs deprecated for 12 months or more and raises the Java baseline for Streams to Java 11.

Keep the route decision on the message type (RouteToEndpoint at assembly/namespace/message-type granularity) and treat the type/namespace routing table as the routing artifact to review; reach for the routing pipeline stage only when a criterion other than message type genuinely drives the decision.

If routing must consult content, put it in a named routing extension (custom route source + UnicastRoutingTable.AddOrReplaceRoutes) rather than in send-site if statements; accept that the routing pipeline stage intercepts all dispatched messages including non-NServiceBus payloads such as audit messages.

Treat route ambiguity as fatal: NServiceBus throws on conflicting routes at startup; the documented best practice for a refreshed route table is to raise a critical error so the endpoint shuts down instead of routing incorrectly.

Do not build priority or multi-lane routing on MakeInstanceUniquelyAddressable + RouteToSpecificInstance; NServiceBus docs explicitly advise against that pattern and against hard-coding discriminators at send sites.

Prefer type-based routing for commands and let the transport do the routing; where a destination genuinely depends on content, express it as data at the dispatch site with a v9 AddMessageRoute<T>((provider, message) => uri) delegate, not by inspecting payloads in every consumer.

Do not build CBR on top of a global EndpointConvention map: conventions are keyed by message type, cannot send one type to two endpoints, and throw on duplicate registration; use message routes or GetSendEndpoint for content-aware dispatch.

Monitor the *_skipped queue: in a type-routed system a misrouted message is moved to <queue>_skipped with its content preserved; an unmonitored _skipped queue makes a misroute look like a consumer that never runs.

Use per-transaction dynamic routing (routing slip itinerary with ExecuteContext/CompensateContext, or a saga state machine) for workflows whose steps depend on message data rather than teaching a CBR about the workflow.

Model the discriminator as a closed union or enum and route with match so routing exhaustiveness is compiler-checked; the wildcard branch should return an error, never silently map to a real destination.
Keep one typed HTTP client per destination so the routing rule is the only place that names a destination and call sites remain type-checked.

Pre-register schemas in CI/CD with auto.register.schemas=false rather than relying on production auto-registration; a misconfigured producer can otherwise redefine the routing surface by registering new schema versions in production.

Prefer backward compatibility as the schema compatibility level: Kafka Streams requires at least backward compatibility for changelog topic replay, and a compatibility level that looks permissive for the schema can be wrong for a routing predicate.

Use topic-based subject naming strategy and avoid RecordNameStrategy or TopicRecordNameStrategy, which allow an unbounded number of types in one topic, breaking ksqlDB, Flink and any router that needs to enumerate the routing domain.
Note that compatibility checks know nothing about actual data in the system: a level that looks permissive for the schema may be wrong for a routing predicate that depends on a specific field value.

Instrument the router with messaging spans using the OTel semantic conventions: emit a producer span on forward and a consumer span on receive, with a link to the message creation context so traces remain coherent across the routing hop.

Because a span can only have a single parent, a CBR that forks to N destinations must use span LINKS rather than child-parent relationships to connect the producer's creation context to each consumer.

A router that republishes without extracting or injecting the original trace context breaks the trace at exactly the hop where observability matters most; propagate the original traceparent through application-properties or message-annotations and never clobber the producer's context.
Route decisions must not be driven by trace context or baggage from the incoming request: baggage has no integrity checks and trace headers can be forged; treat them as read-only metadata.
Be aware that OTel messaging semantic conventions are still in Development status; pin attribute and span names with OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN to avoid dashboard breakage when names change.
Prefer correlation filters over SQL filters in Azure Service Bus: SQL filter rules cause lower overall message throughput at the subscription, topic and namespace level.

In AWS SNS, distinguish between unmatched payloads (NumberOfNotificationsFilteredOut-MessageBody) and malformed JSON (NumberOfNotificationsFilteredOut-InvalidMessageBody); route the latter to a DLQ so schema drift and JSON corruption are separate, monitorable failure modes.

In Istio and Envoy, routing rules are evaluated per request in the sidecar; prefer exact header matches over regex for high-throughput paths and always include a catch-all route block at the bottom of the match list.

Mesh-layer routing is not a security boundary: a policy mismatch between Envoy and the backend can lead to unexpected rejection or a policy bypass; use default-deny, strict mTLS, and ALLOW-with-positive-matching.
Route decisions expressed as CloudEvents type strings serve multiple consumers simultaneously; versioning of the type string must be deliberate to avoid silent re-classification.

Semantic or learned routing (routing based on embeddings or ML models) turns routing errors into quality errors with no delivery-error signal; validate routing policy offline, monitor achieved-vs-intended distribution, and have a documented rollback path.

Adaptive latency-based routing can silently degrade to weighted random selection if the latency cache suffers from lost updates; monitor the effective routing distribution, not only the configured policy.

When routing LLM requests across providers or regions, account for session affinity (provider-side prompt caching, data-residency rules) and model-specific retry/fallback policies as first-class routing concerns.

In type-routed .NET stacks and stream processors there is no broker-side body filter: a content-based route is always type/topic route plus application code, so the routing matrix must be unit-tested as such.

Decide explicitly between transport/type routing, send-pipeline destination resolution, and in-process predicate tables; mixing mechanisms in one flow is how the same logical route ends up expressed twice and drifts.
AWS IoT SQL rules cannot see comments, attribute names with spaces, or escaped-JSON string bodies; design the routing payload schema to match the rule engine's constraints.

Dapr pub/sub CEL expressions cannot compare against time (before/after 'now') and can only access nested JSON values, not JSON-escaped-in-a-string payloads; design the message shape to match what the DSL can see.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (Addison-Wesley, 2003), Content-Based Router (Message Routing chapter) - the canonical reference; the router examines message content and routes to the appropriate channel; routing logic must stay maintainable as the router becomes a frequent change point.

https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-24-how-to-implement-content-based-routing-in-istio/view - practical guide to Istio VirtualService HTTP match rules for content-based routing in service mesh.
https://statuscodefyi.com/guides/gateway-request-routing-guide/ - covers API gateway content-based routing for GraphQL and gRPC, performance tradeoffs of body parsing vs header-based routing.

https://udidahan.com/2011/03/20/careful-with-content-based-routing/ - Udi Dahan's cautionary note on CBR creating a hub-and-spoke bottleneck and maintenance burden, arguing for alternatives like physical one-to-many distribution.
https://www.ioriver.io - What Is Content-Based Routing? Benefits & Best Practices overview.

https://activemq.apache.org/components/classic/documentation/selectors - JMS message selectors in SQL-92 over headers and properties for content-based routing; XPath selectors over XML bodies require the Xalan library, and STOMP string properties need convert_string_expressions for numeric comparisons.

https://activemq.apache.org/components/classic/documentation/should-i-deploy-enterprise-integration-patterns-in-the-broker-or-another-application - official tradeoff analysis for deploying the router inside the broker versus a separate application.
